title: Hadith, Law and the Golden Age
bigQuestion: How did Muslims build a way of life from the Qur'an and the Prophet's example, and why did one tradition grow into many schools, branches and centers of learning?

story.title: The Long Road of a Book
story.kicker: One imagined book, three real cities, and eight hundred years of readers who left their notes in its margins.
paragraphs: Baghdad, around the year 900. On a street of booksellers near the Tigris River, a copyist sits cross-legged with a reed pen and a stack of paper. Paper is still fairly new here; the city's mills have been making it for about a century, and it has made books cheaper than ever before. He is copying an Arabic book on the stars, part of it translated from Greek. He begins, as Muslim copyists do, with the words In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

Córdoba, around the year 1000. The book has traveled west with a merchant, across North Africa and over the narrow strait into Spain. A young student reads it by lamplight, in a city with more books than almost any other in Europe. In the margin he writes a small correction to one of the tables, and a note that his teacher disagrees with the author. Down the street, Jewish and Christian scholars read Arabic too, because it is the language of learning.

Timbuktu, around the year 1500. The book has crossed the Sahara on a camel, packed among bars of salt, and been sold in a market where gold from the south meets goods from the north. A family of scholars buys it. The father teaches law and astronomy to students who sit in the courtyard of a mud-brick mosque. He adds his own note in the margin, and his sons and grandsons add theirs. The book goes into a wooden chest with hundreds of others.

Timbuktu, 2012. Armed groups have taken over the city, and some of them want to destroy the old manuscripts. Quietly, at night, librarians and families pack the books into metal trunks and rice sacks and send them south by car, by donkey cart and by boat to the capital, Bamako. The book in this story is imagined, but that rescue was real, and hundreds of thousands of real manuscripts survived it.

Follow a book like this one and you meet most of this chapter. Its margins hold arguments about law and about the Prophet's sayings. Its readers were Sunni and Shia, jurists and mystics. Its science passed from Greek into Arabic and later into Latin. This chapter looks at how Muslims built law and learning on the Qur'an and the Prophet's example, and how one tradition grew many branches.
story.think: The imagined book passed through Muslim, Jewish and Christian hands in three cities. What can the life of a single manuscript show that a list of dates cannot?

sections.title: The Prophet's Example and the Law

lessons.title: Hadith and Sunnah
lessons.mainIdea: The Sunnah is the Prophet's example, known through hadith reports that scholars collected and tested, and it is the second source of Islamic guidance after the Qur'an.
reading: The Qur'an tells Muslims many times to pray, but it does not spell out every movement of the prayer or how many times to bow. Muslims learned those details by watching Muhammad. The Qur'an itself calls the Messenger of God a fine example to follow. His way of living, speaking and deciding is called the *Sunnah*, meaning the beaten path or custom. For most Muslims it is the second source of guidance after the Qur'an.

The Sunnah is known through the *hadith*, reports of what the Prophet said, did or approved. Each hadith has two parts. The *isnad* is the chain of people who passed it on: one person heard it from a second, who heard it from a third, who heard the Prophet. The matn is the text of the report itself. After Muhammad's death, thousands of reports circulated, and some were invented to support one side in a dispute.

So scholars built a science for testing reports. They studied every person in each chain. Was he or she honest? Did they have a good memory? Could they really have met the person they quoted? A report judged fully reliable is *sahih*, meaning sound; others are graded good or weak. In the 800s, al-Bukhari (died 870) and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (died 875) compiled the collections Sunni Muslims trust most, each called a Sahih. Shia Muslims rely on their own collections, which give special weight to reports passed down through the Prophet's family.

Hadith shape ordinary life: how to wash before prayer, what to say after a sneeze, eating with the right hand, and the teaching that even a smile for another person counts as charity. Keep one distinction clear. Muslims believe the Qur'an is the word of God. Hadith are human reports about the Prophet, and scholars have always weighed them, sometimes reaching different conclusions about the same report.

words.d: the example of the Prophet Muhammad, his words, deeds and approvals, which Muslims follow as the second source of guidance
a report of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did or approved; also the whole body of such reports
the chain of people who passed a hadith down from the Prophet's time
sound; a hadith that scholars judge fully reliable, and the title of the most trusted Sunni collections

look.title: Actions Are Judged by Intentions
look.text: Actions are judged only by their intentions, and each person will have what he intended. Whoever migrated for the sake of God and His Messenger, his migration was for God and His Messenger. Whoever migrated to gain something of this world, or to marry, his migration was for what he migrated for.
look.cite: Hadith reported by Umar ibn al-Khattab, the first hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari (9th century), in a plain paraphrase
look.prompt: This hadith mentions the hijra from chapter 9. Why might al-Bukhari have chosen a report about intentions to open a whole collection about how to live?

check.why: A hadith is a report of the Prophet's words, deeds or approval; together the reports make his Sunnah, or example, known.

check.why: The isnad is the chain of transmitters; the text itself is called the matn.

check.q: How do Muslims distinguish the Qur'an from the hadith?

They believe the hadith are older than the Qur'an
They consider both to be the exact words of God
They read hadith only in translation and the Qur'an only in Arabic
check.why: Muslims hold the Qur'an to be God's word; hadith are reports about Muhammad, graded by scholars as sound, good or weak.

lessons.title: Sharia and Fiqh
lessons.mainIdea: Sharia is the divine guidance Muslims believe God has given; fiqh is the human effort of scholars to understand it, and it covers worship and daily life far more than courts.
reading: A Muslim college student in Chicago wants to buy a car, but she does not want a loan that charges interest. Many scholars read the Qur'an's ban on riba, usury, as covering ordinary interest, while others disagree. She asks what is permitted. That is a question about *sharia*. The word first meant the path to a watering place, a route to life-giving water in the desert. Muslims use it for the whole of God's guidance for human life: prayer, fasting, family, business, food and manners, with crime and punishment a smaller part.

Muslim scholars separate sharia from *fiqh*, literally understanding, the human work of figuring out what that guidance requires in a real case. Sharia, Muslims believe, is perfect; fiqh is done by people and can disagree. In classical Sunni theory, jurists draw on four sources: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, *ijma*, the consensus of scholars, and *qiyas*, reasoning by analogy. The Qur'an forbids wine, for example, and by analogy most jurists extended the ban to other intoxicants. Shia jurists use a similar method, with a larger role for reason and for the teachings of the imams.

Jurists sort acts into five categories: required, such as the five daily prayers; recommended, such as extra prayers; permitted, which covers most of daily life; disliked, such as wasting water while washing for prayer; and forbidden, such as theft or eating pork. A scholar qualified to answer questions is a mufti, and the answer is a *fatwa*, a legal opinion. A fatwa is not automatically binding. News reports sometimes use the word as if it meant a death sentence, but most fatwas answer ordinary questions about prayer, money or marriage.

Countries today differ widely. Some, such as Saudi Arabia and Iran, base much of their national law on their own reading of sharia. Many Muslim-majority countries apply it mainly to family matters like marriage and inheritance, alongside civil law codes. In the United States, Muslims follow sharia in personal practice, such as prayer, fasting and halal food, much as observant Jews follow Jewish law, while living under American law. Debates about sharia, including over punishments and the rights of women, continue among Muslims themselves.

words.d: the path of divine guidance for all of life that Muslims believe God has given; originally, the path to a watering place
Islamic jurisprudence; the human effort of scholars to understand and apply sharia
the consensus of qualified scholars, one of the classical sources of Sunni law
reasoning by analogy from an existing ruling to a new case
a legal opinion given by a qualified scholar in answer to a question; not automatically binding

look.title: Five Categories
look.text: Here are five actions: praying the noon prayer; giving extra charity beyond zakat; eating an apple; running the faucet far longer than needed while washing for prayer; drinking a glass of wine. Muslim jurists sort every act into required, recommended, permitted, disliked or forbidden.
look.prompt: Place each action in one of the five categories. Then invent a modern case, such as an energy drink or an online loan, and explain how a jurist might use qiyas to decide it.

check.why: Sharia is believed to be God's perfect guidance; fiqh is scholars' fallible understanding of it, which is why jurists can disagree.

lessons.title: The Schools of Law
lessons.mainIdea: Sunni Muslims recognize four main schools of law and most Shia follow the Ja'fari school; each is a respected tradition of reasoning, not a separate religion.
reading: Watch the rows of worshipers in a large mosque and you may notice small differences. Some fold their hands on the chest, some just below the navel, and many Maliki Muslims and most Shia let their arms hang at their sides. These differences often come from the *madhhab*, the school of law, that a person follows. Each school grew from the teaching of an early scholar and his students in the 700s and 800s, and each built its own body of rulings.

Sunni Muslims recognize four schools. The *Hanafi* school, named for Abu Hanifa of Kufa (died 767), is the largest, strong in Turkey, Central Asia and South Asia. The Maliki school, from Malik ibn Anas of Medina (died 795), dominates North and West Africa. The Shafi'i school, from al-Shafi'i (died 820), is strong in parts of Egypt, East Africa, and Southeast Asia, including Indonesia and Malaysia. The Hanbali school, from Ahmad ibn Hanbal of Baghdad (died 855), is the smallest and strongest in Saudi Arabia.

Most Shia Muslims follow the *Ja'fari* school, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq (died 765), whom Shia honor as the sixth Imam. Twelver Shia also practice something distinctive: each believer chooses a living senior scholar, a *marja*, meaning source to follow, and follows that scholar's rulings. The best-known marjas today live in the shrine cities of Najaf in Iraq and Qom in Iran, and they answer questions sent from believers around the world, including from Chicago.

The schools agree on the essentials: the Five Pillars, the ban on pork and alcohol, and the authority of the Qur'an and Sunnah. They differ on details, and classical scholars treated that as normal. A saying often repeated among Muslims calls difference of opinion among scholars a mercy. Today many Muslims follow one school, while others, especially in the West, draw on several or follow reformers who urge a return directly to the Qur'an and hadith.

words.d: a school of Islamic law that grew from the teaching of an early scholar; plural madhhabs
the largest Sunni school of law, named for Abu Hanifa, strong in Turkey, Central Asia and South Asia
the school of law followed by most Shia Muslims, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq
in Twelver Shia Islam, a senior living scholar whose rulings a believer chooses to follow

lessons.title: The Question of Succession
lessons.mainIdea: When Muhammad died in 632, Muslims disagreed about who should lead; Sunnis accept the chosen caliphs, while Shia believe leadership belonged to Ali and the Prophet's family.
reading: Medina, June 632. The Prophet has died. He left no surviving son and, Sunnis hold, named no successor. A group of leading Muslims met and chose Abu Bakr, Muhammad's close friend and father-in-law, as *caliph*, from the Arabic khalifa, successor or deputy. The caliph led the community in politics, war and prayer, but he did not receive revelation. Muslims believe prophecy ended with Muhammad.

The name *Sunni* comes from ahl al-sunna, the people of the Sunnah and of the community. Sunnis honor the first four caliphs, Abu Bakr (632 to 634), Umar (634 to 644), Uthman (644 to 656) and Ali (656 to 661), as the Rightly Guided Caliphs. In Sunni thinking, the community should be led by a qualified Muslim whom it accepts. Later caliphs, such as the Umayyads in Damascus and the Abbasids in Baghdad, ruled great empires.

The name *Shia* comes from Shi'at Ali, the party of Ali. Ali was Muhammad's cousin, one of the first to accept Islam, and the husband of the Prophet's daughter Fatima. Shia Muslims believe the Prophet named Ali as his successor at a place called Ghadir Khumm, on the way home from his last pilgrimage. Sunnis accept a report of that event but read its key word as friend, not ruler. For Shia, rightful leadership belongs to a line of *Imams* descended from Ali and Fatima.

Today, by common estimates, about 85 to 90 percent of the world's Muslims are Sunni and about 10 to 15 percent are Shia. Shia are the majority in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Bahrain, with large communities in Lebanon, Pakistan and India. The two share the Qur'an, the Five Pillars and the hajj, where they pray side by side. The split began as a question of leadership, though over centuries each developed its own law, holidays and practices.

words.d: from khalifa, successor; in Sunni Islam, a leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad, without prophetic authority
the majority branch of Islam, from the people of the Sunnah; honors the first four caliphs as rightly guided
the branch of Islam that holds that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants; from the party of Ali
in Shia belief, the divinely guided leaders of the community descended from Ali and Fatima

lessons.title: Karbala and Shia Devotion
lessons.mainIdea: The death of Ali's son Husayn at Karbala in 680 became the central story of Shia memory, relived each year on Ashura.
reading: On the tenth day of the month of Muharram, Shia Muslims in Karachi, in Iraq and in Chicago gather dressed in black to hear a story many of them know by heart. In 680, Husayn, the Prophet's grandson through Ali and Fatima, refused to pledge loyalty to Yazid, the Umayyad caliph. He set out for Kufa in Iraq with his family and a small band of companions. At *Karbala*, near the Euphrates River, a far larger army surrounded them and cut them off from water. Husayn and most of the men were killed; the women and children were taken captive.

Shia Muslims remember that day as *Ashura*. Communities hold gatherings where reciters retell the story and listeners weep. There are processions, poems of mourning, and in Iran traditional passion plays that reenact the battle. Many mourners beat their chests in rhythm; a few practice harsher forms of mourning that many Shia scholars discourage, and some communities hold blood drives instead. Sunni Muslims also mark Ashura, often with a voluntary fast, recalling a hadith that links the day to Moses and the Israelites being saved from Pharaoh.

Shia Muslims believe a line of Imams followed Ali. The largest branch, the *Twelvers*, count twelve. They believe the twelfth, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into hiding in the 870s, a state called *occultation*, and will return at the end of time to fill the world with justice. Other Shia branches include the Ismailis, whose living leader holds the title Aga Khan, and the Zaydis of Yemen.

Shia devotion centers on shrines of the Imams: Ali's tomb at Najaf, Husayn's at Karbala, and the eighth Imam's at Mashhad in Iran. Each year, forty days after Ashura, millions of pilgrims walk to Karbala, one of the largest gatherings on earth. Themes of martyrdom, standing against injustice and love for the Prophet's family run through Shia life. Sunnis, too, honor Ali and Husayn as members of the Prophet's family.

words.d: the place in Iraq where Husayn was killed in 680; today a Shia shrine city
the tenth day of Muharram, when Shia Muslims mourn Husayn's death; many Sunnis mark it with a fast
the largest Shia branch, which recognizes twelve Imams
in Twelver belief, the hidden state of the twelfth Imam, who is expected to return at the end of time

look.title: A Story of Defeat, Retold
look.text: Imagine a community that retells, every year, the story of a small group who kept their principles against a far larger army and lost. Everyone listening knows how it ends. They weep anyway, and many leave saying they want to stand up for what is right in their own lives.
look.prompt: Why might a community retell a defeat rather than a victory? What values does the Karbala story carry for Shia Muslims, and what story works in a similar way in another tradition or in American history?

lessons.title: Sufism: The Inner Path
lessons.mainIdea: Sufism is the mystical side of Islam, in which Muslims seek direct experience of God's love through remembrance, poetry and a master's guidance.
reading: In Konya, Turkey, men in tall felt hats and long white skirts turn slowly to the music of a reed flute, the right palm raised toward heaven and the left turned toward earth. They belong to the Mevlevi order, founded by followers of the poet Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207 to 1273), who is buried in Konya. For them the turning, called sema, is a form of prayer. Rumi's poems, often in loose English versions, are widely read in the United States today.

*Sufism*, tasawwuf in Arabic, is the mystical path within Islam: the effort to know God directly, from the heart, and not only through outward rules. Most Sufis have kept the law carefully and seen it as the doorway to the inner path. The name probably comes from suf, wool, the rough cloth early ascetics wore. An early Sufi, Rabi'a al-Adawiyya of Basra (died 801), is remembered for teaching that God should be loved for God's own sake.

The central Sufi practice is *dhikr*, remembrance: repeating the names of God or a phrase such as la ilaha illa Allah, there is no god but God, alone or in a circle, often in rhythm with the breath. Sufis join a *tariqa*, an order or path, and learn from a *sheikh*, a master who guides disciples. Orders such as the Qadiriyya, Naqshbandiyya and Chishtiyya spread across three continents, and Sufi teachers helped spread Islam in South Asia, Africa and Southeast Asia. There are both Sunni and Shia Sufis.

Al-Ghazali (died 1111), a leading scholar in Baghdad, left his teaching post during a personal crisis and later wrote that Sufi experience and the law belong together; many Muslims accepted his view. Not all Muslims embrace Sufism. Some reform movements, including Salafi movements and the Wahhabi movement in Saudi Arabia, criticize practices such as visiting saints' tombs, which they see as risking shirk. Sufis reply that they honor saints but worship God alone. A student of religion describes both views.

words.d: the mystical path within Islam, seeking direct, inward knowledge and love of God; tasawwuf in Arabic
remembrance; the Sufi practice of repeating God's names or a sacred phrase
a Sufi order, or path, with its own master, practices and line of teachers
in Sufism, a master who guides disciples on the path; also a general title of respect

lessons.title: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: In Abbasid Baghdad, scholars of many faiths translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, preserving them and building on them.
reading: In 762, the caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the Tigris River and laid it out as a great circle: Baghdad. Within a century it was one of the largest cities in the world, a crossroads of trade from China to Spain. Paper, a Chinese invention, was being made in Baghdad by the late 700s. It was far cheaper than parchment, so books became cheaper and more plentiful, and booksellers' shops lined whole streets.

The *Abbasid* caliphs, who ruled from Baghdad, sponsored a *translation movement* that lasted about two centuries. Scholars translated the works of Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Galen and Hippocrates from Greek, often through Syriac, along with books from Persian and Sanskrit. Many translators were Christians, such as the physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq (died 873), who with his students translated much of Galen's medicine. Jewish, Sabian and Muslim scholars worked alongside them. The caliph al-Ma'mun (ruled 813 to 833) was an especially famous patron.

Al-Ma'mun's court is linked with the *House of Wisdom*, Bayt al-Hikma in Arabic, a royal library where scholars read, copied and discussed books. Historians debate how large and organized it was; some describe it mainly as a library rather than a university. What is clear is that scholars in Baghdad did not only preserve the Greek works. They checked them, argued with them and corrected them.

Why did this happen? Historians give several reasons: the Qur'an's repeated call to reflect on the signs of God in nature; practical needs such as calendars, prayer times, the qibla, inheritance math and medicine; and the prestige that learning brought a ruler. The golden age is usually dated from the 700s to the 1200s. In 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad and killed the last Abbasid caliph there, but learning continued in Cairo, Samarkand, Istanbul and Mughal India.

words.d: the dynasty of caliphs that ruled from Baghdad from 750 until the Mongol conquest of 1258
the effort, from about the 700s to the 900s, to translate Greek, Persian and Indian learning into Arabic
Bayt al-Hikma, a royal library and center of scholarship in Abbasid Baghdad

lessons.title: Algebra, Stars and Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars writing in Arabic advanced mathematics, astronomy, optics and medicine, and words like algebra and algorithm still carry their traces.
reading: When you solve x + 5 = 12 by subtracting 5 from both sides, you are using a method explained by al-Khwarizmi (about 780 to 850), a scholar in Baghdad. Around 820 he wrote a book on calculating by al-jabr, restoring, and al-muqabala, balancing. Al-jabr became our word *algebra*. His name, written in Latin as Algoritmi, gave us *algorithm*. Another of his books spread the Indian system of place-value numerals with zero; Europeans later called them Arabic numerals, though they began in India.

Astronomy had religious uses. Muslims needed to set the times of the five prayers, find the qibla, and sight the new moon that begins each month of the lunar calendar. Astronomers built observatories, such as those at Maragha in Iran (1259) and Samarkand (1420s), improved Ptolemy's tables, and perfected the *astrolabe*, a brass instrument for measuring the positions of the sun and stars. Many star names are Arabic, including Aldebaran, Betelgeuse, Altair and Vega.

Cities such as Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo built hospitals, called *bimaristan*, with separate wards for different illnesses; many treated patients without charge. The physician al-Razi (died about 925) wrote one of the earliest clear accounts telling smallpox from measles. Ibn Sina (980 to 1037) wrote the Canon of Medicine, which was taught in European universities for centuries. In Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham (died about 1040) used experiments to argue that we see because light enters the eye.

These scholars were Arabs, Persians, Central Asians and others; some were Christian or Jewish, like the physician and philosopher Maimonides. Their books were later translated into Latin in Spain and Sicily, where Ibn Sina became Avicenna and al-Razi became Rhazes. Historians describe this as a bridge from ancient Greek science to the European Renaissance, and they stress that it was original work, not only storage for Greek ideas.

words.d: the branch of math that solves for unknowns; from al-jabr, restoring, in al-Khwarizmi's book title
a step-by-step method for solving a problem; from the Latin form of al-Khwarizmi's name
a brass instrument for measuring the positions of the sun and stars, used for time and direction
a hospital in the medieval Islamic world, often with separate wards for different illnesses

look.title: Words That Traveled
look.text: Some English words that came from Arabic: algebra (from al-jabr), algorithm (from al-Khwarizmi), zero (from sifr, empty), alchemy and chemistry (from al-kimiya), alcohol (from al-kuhl), and the star names Aldebaran and Altair. Several begin with al-, the Arabic word for the.
look.prompt: Choose three of these words. What does each suggest about which fields of knowledge moved from Arabic into European languages, and why might the Arabic word have been kept?

check.q: Where does the word algebra come from?
choices: From the Greek name of Euclid
From the Latin word for balance
From the Persian word for number
From al-jabr, restoring, in the title of al-Khwarizmi's book
check.why: Al-Khwarizmi's book on al-jabr and al-muqabala, written around 820, gave algebra its name.

check.q: Why did astronomy matter to Muslim religious practice?
choices: The Qur'an requires Muslims to name the stars
It helped set prayer times, find the qibla and sight the new moon for the lunar calendar
It was needed to build the Kaaba
It fixed the hajj to the solar year
check.why: Prayer times, the direction of Mecca and the start of each lunar month all depend on the sky.

check.q: Who wrote the Canon of Medicine, used in European universities for centuries?
choices: Al-Khwarizmi
Hunayn ibn Ishaq
Ibn Sina, known in Latin as Avicenna
Rumi
check.why: Ibn Sina, or Avicenna, wrote the Canon of Medicine; Latin translations made it a standard textbook in Europe.

lessons.title: Córdoba and Timbuktu
lessons.mainIdea: Learning flourished far from Baghdad, in al-Andalus in Spain and in the West African city of Timbuktu, where manuscripts are still kept.
reading: In 711, Muslim armies crossed from North Africa into Spain, and the Muslim-ruled lands there became known as *al-Andalus*. In 756, Abd al-Rahman, an Umayyad prince who had escaped the Abbasids, set up his rule at Córdoba. Its Great Mosque, begun in 785, is famous for its forest of red-and-white striped arches. By the 900s Córdoba was one of the largest cities in Europe, and the library of the caliph al-Hakam II was said to hold hundreds of thousands of books.

Jews and Christians in al-Andalus lived as *dhimmi*, protected communities who paid a special tax and had fewer rights than Muslims, but kept their own worship and courts. Many historians use the Spanish word *convivencia*, living together, for the exchange among the three faiths; others stress its limits and periods of persecution. Both are part of the record. The Muslim philosopher Ibn Rushd (1126 to 1198) and the Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138 to 1204), who wrote mostly in Arabic, were both born in Córdoba. Castile conquered the city in 1236, and the mosque became a cathedral.

Timbuktu stands at the edge of the Sahara near the Niger River. Under the Mali and later the Songhay empires, it became a market where gold, salt and books were traded. Mali's ruler Mansa Musa made the hajj in 1324 and passed through Cairo with so much gold that writers described it for generations. He brought scholars home with him, and the mud-brick Djinguereyber mosque, begun in his time, still stands. Teachers at mosques such as Sankore taught Maliki law, Arabic grammar, astronomy and medicine.

Timbuktu's families collected *manuscript* books for centuries: Qur'ans, law, astronomy, poetry and business letters, some in African languages written in Arabic script. In 2012, armed groups occupied the city. Librarians and families smuggled hundreds of thousands of manuscripts south to Bamako; a few thousand were burned, but most were saved. Timbuktu is a reminder that the golden age of Islamic learning was African as well as Arab and Persian.

words.d: the Muslim-ruled lands of the Iberian Peninsula, in today's Spain and Portugal, from 711 to 1492
a member of a protected non-Muslim community, such as Jews and Christians, under Muslim rule
Spanish for living together; historians' term for the exchange among Muslims, Jews and Christians in medieval Spain
a book or document written by hand

look.title: Two Views of al-Andalus
look.text: Historian A: In Córdoba, Muslims, Jews and Christians shared a language, read the same books and built a brilliant culture together. Historian B: Jews and Christians there paid a special tax, could not build new houses of worship freely, and at times faced violence. Both historians cite real evidence.
look.prompt: Can both historians be right? What kinds of evidence would you look for to decide how life in al-Andalus changed over time and from group to group?

check.q: What was al-Andalus?
choices: The Muslim-ruled lands of the Iberian Peninsula, in today's Spain and Portugal
A school of law in West Africa
The capital of the Abbasid caliphs
A Sufi order in Turkey
check.why: Al-Andalus was Muslim-ruled Iberia, with Córdoba as its great early center.

check.q: Why is Mansa Musa remembered?
choices: He founded Baghdad
He translated Aristotle into Arabic
He conquered Córdoba in 1236
His hajj in 1324 displayed Mali's wealth, and he brought scholars back to his empire
check.why: Mansa Musa's gold amazed Cairo during his 1324 hajj, and he brought scholars and builders home to Mali.

check.q: What happened to Timbuktu's manuscripts when armed groups occupied the city in 2012?
choices: All were burned
Librarians smuggled most of them to safety in Bamako, though some were destroyed
They were sold to European museums
They were sent to Baghdad
check.why: Families and librarians moved hundreds of thousands of manuscripts to Bamako; a few thousand were lost.

lessons.title: The Art of the Written Word
lessons.mainIdea: Because Muslims revere the Qur'an as God's word, calligraphy became the most honored Islamic art, joined by geometric pattern and the arabesque.
reading: Look up inside the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed around 691, and you see bands of gold Arabic letters, among the earliest dated inscriptions of Qur'anic verses. Islamic religious art usually avoids images of living beings, and the written word takes their place. *Calligraphy*, beautiful writing, became the most honored art of all, because it gives visible form to words Muslims believe God spoke.

Calligraphers developed many styles. *Kufic* is angular and was used in early copies of the Qur'an. *Naskh* is rounded and easy to read, and it became the standard hand for copying books. Thuluth is large and flowing, often used on mosque walls. Calligraphers trained for years under a master, cut their own reed pens, and measured each letter in dots made by the pen's tip. Ottoman sultans signed decrees with a tughra, an elaborate calligraphic emblem of the ruler's name.

Two other elements appear everywhere. Geometric patterns start from circles and grow into stars and polygons that seem to repeat without end; many Muslims see in them the order and unity of creation, though artists' own intentions varied. The *arabesque* is a pattern of winding vines and leaves. You can see all three at the Alhambra in Granada, in the tiled mosques of Isfahan, and at the Taj Mahal in Agra, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in the 1600s as a tomb for his wife, with Qur'an verses inlaid in stone.

Not all Islamic art avoids figures. Persian, Turkish and Mughal painters illustrated books of history and poetry with detailed scenes of people and animals, and some even depicted the Prophet, often with his face veiled. Views on images vary by place, period and community; avoidance is strongest in mosques and in copies of the Qur'an. Today calligraphy is still thriving, from traditional masters in Istanbul to young artists painting Arabic letters on city walls.

words.d: the art of beautiful writing; in Islamic tradition, the most honored art
an angular style of Arabic script used in early copies of the Qur'an and in architecture
a rounded, readable style of Arabic script that became standard for copying books
a decorative pattern of winding vines, leaves and tendrils

look.title: An Oath by the Pen
look.text: Nun. By the pen, and by what they write.
look.cite: Qur'an, Sura 68 (al-Qalam, the Pen), verse 1, in a plain paraphrase
look.prompt: Here the Qur'an swears by the pen, and in chapter 9 the first revealed verses praised God who taught by the pen. Why might a tradition with verses like these make writing its highest art?

check.q: Why did calligraphy become the most honored art in Islamic tradition?
choices: Paint was forbidden in all Muslim lands
It was the only art the caliphs could afford
It gives visible form to the words Muslims believe God spoke in the Qur'an
It was invented by al-Khwarizmi
check.why: Because the Qur'an is revered as God's word, writing it beautifully became the highest form of art.

check.q: Which description matches the Kufic script?
choices: An angular style used in early copies of the Qur'an
A rounded style used for everyday books
A Sufi dance
A Persian style of painting
check.why: Kufic is the angular early script; Naskh is the rounded hand that became standard for books.

check.q: Which statement about images in Islamic art is accurate?
choices: No Muslim artist has ever painted a person
Images of people are required in mosques
Only Shia Muslims practice calligraphy
Figures are avoided mainly in mosques and Qur'ans, while some Persian, Turkish and Mughal books were richly illustrated
check.why: Avoidance of images is strongest in religious settings; illustrated manuscripts from Persia, Turkey and Mughal India show people and animals.

lessons.title: Muslims in America and Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Islam has been part of American history since enslaved West Africans arrived, and Chicago today is home to one of the country's largest and most diverse Muslim communities.
reading: In 1831, in North Carolina, an enslaved man named Omar ibn Said wrote a short account of his life in Arabic. Born in West Africa, in what is now Senegal, he had studied the Qur'an and other books before he was captured. Historians estimate that a significant share of the Africans enslaved in the Americas were Muslim. Some kept praying and fasting in secret, but very little of their practice survived slavery.

Later, Arab immigrants from the Ottoman Empire, especially from what is now Syria and Lebanon, arrived from the late 1800s. A mosque built in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, in 1934 is one of the oldest still standing. The *Nation of Islam*, founded in Detroit in 1930, was led for decades from Chicago by Elijah Muhammad. It preached Black self-reliance and taught beliefs that most Muslims worldwide considered outside Islam. After his death in 1975, his son Warith Deen Mohammed led most members into Sunni Islam; Louis Farrakhan later rebuilt a separate Nation of Islam, still based in Chicago.

The *Immigration Act of 1965* ended quotas that had favored Europeans. Muslims then came from South Asia, the Arab world, Iran, Africa and elsewhere, later joined by refugees from Bosnia, Somalia, Iraq and Syria. The Pew Research Center estimated about 3.45 million Muslims in the United States in 2017, about 1 percent of the population. Pew found that no single racial or ethnic group makes up a majority, and Black Americans are a large share of U.S.-born Muslims.

Chicago reflects all of this. There are South Asian shops on Devon Avenue, Arab American neighborhoods on the Southwest Side and in suburbs like Bridgeview, Bosnian and West African mosques, and African American communities with roots in the 1930s. The Inner-City Muslim Action Network, *IMAN*, founded in 1997 on the Southwest Side, runs a health clinic and arts programs open to all. After September 11, 2001, many American Muslims reported discrimination, and civil rights groups still track such incidents.

words.d: an African American religious movement founded in Detroit in 1930 and led from Chicago; distinct from mainstream Sunni and Shia Islam
a U.S. law that ended national-origin quotas and opened immigration from Asia, Africa and the Middle East
the Inner-City Muslim Action Network, a Chicago organization founded in 1997 that offers health care, arts and community programs

look.title: Nations and Tribes
look.text: O humankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you into nations and tribes so that you may come to know one another. The most honored of you in the sight of God is the one most mindful of God.
look.cite: Qur'an, Sura 49 (al-Hujurat), verse 13, in a plain paraphrase
look.prompt: Chicago's Muslims trace their roots to dozens of countries and to American history itself. How might a mosque community use this verse to think about its own diversity? Recall what Malcolm X wrote after his hajj.

check.q: Who was Omar ibn Said?
choices: The founder of the Nation of Islam
An enslaved West African Muslim scholar who wrote an account of his life in Arabic in 1831
The first imam of the Cedar Rapids mosque
A translator of the Qur'an into English
check.why: Omar ibn Said, enslaved in North Carolina, wrote his life story in Arabic, evidence of Islam's early presence in America.

check.q: What happened to the Nation of Islam after Elijah Muhammad died in 1975?
choices: It moved its headquarters to Mecca
It merged with the Ismailis
His son Warith Deen Mohammed led most members toward Sunni Islam, and Louis Farrakhan later rebuilt a separate Nation
It ended completely and left no successors
check.why: Warith Deen Mohammed brought most followers into Sunni Islam; Farrakhan revived the Nation of Islam, still based in Chicago.

check.q: According to the Pew Research Center, which statement describes American Muslims?
choices: No single racial or ethnic group makes up a majority
Almost all are recent immigrants from one country
They make up about a quarter of the U.S. population
Nearly all are Shia
check.why: Pew found American Muslims to be highly diverse, about 1 percent of the population, with no majority group.

review.q: Which pair correctly matches a source of Islamic law with its meaning?
choices: Isnad: the consensus of scholars
Qiyas: the chain of transmitters
Fatwa: the Prophet's example
Ijma: the consensus of scholars
review.why: Ijma is scholarly consensus; qiyas is analogy, the isnad is a hadith's chain, and a fatwa is a legal opinion.

review.q: A student writes that sharia is simply a list of criminal punishments. What would a scholar of Islam correct?
choices: Sharia, as Muslims understand it, covers worship, family, business, food and manners, and criminal law is a small part
Nothing; the statement is accurate
Sharia covers only prayer and fasting
Sharia is another name for the hadith
review.why: Sharia means God's guidance for all of life; most of fiqh concerns worship, family and daily dealings.

review.q: What was the original disagreement between Sunni and Shia Muslims about?
choices: Whether to pray five times a day
Who should lead the Muslim community after Muhammad's death
Whether the Qur'an should be translated
Which direction to face in prayer
review.why: The split began over succession: Sunnis accepted the chosen caliphs, and Shia held that Ali should lead.

review.q: Which set of figures belongs with Sufism?
choices: Abu Hanifa, Malik and al-Shafi'i
Al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina and al-Razi
Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, al-Ghazali and Rumi
Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman
review.why: Rabi'a, al-Ghazali and Rumi are central to Sufism; the other sets are jurists, scientists and caliphs.

review.q: Which statement best describes the House of Wisdom in Baghdad?
choices: A mosque where the Qur'an was first compiled
A Sufi lodge in Konya
A school of law founded by Ahmad ibn Hanbal
A royal library and center of scholarship linked to translating Greek works into Arabic
review.why: The House of Wisdom was an Abbasid royal library tied to the translation movement under caliphs like al-Ma'mun.

review.q: How did the works of Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd reach European universities?
choices: Through Latin translations made in places such as Toledo
Through English translations made in 1611
Through the Mongol conquest of Baghdad
They were written in Latin to begin with
review.why: Scholars in Spain and Sicily translated Arabic works into Latin, where Ibn Sina became Avicenna and Ibn Rushd Averroes.

review.q: Which city is correctly matched with its role in this chapter?
choices: Karbala: capital of the Abbasid caliphs
Timbuktu: a West African center of trade and scholarship with family manuscript libraries
Córdoba: site of Husayn's death
Baghdad: home of the Djinguereyber mosque
review.why: Timbuktu's families kept manuscripts for centuries; Karbala is where Husayn died, and Baghdad was the Abbasid capital.

review.q: Why does a student of religion write that Shia Muslims believe the Prophet designated Ali, rather than stating it as fact?
choices: Because Ali never existed
Because Shia Muslims do not care about history
Because Sunni and Shia Muslims read the historical reports differently, and the course describes beliefs without taking sides
Because the Qur'an names Ali as the first caliph
review.why: Sunnis and Shia interpret the reports about Ghadir Khumm differently, so an academic study attributes each view to its holders.
